blueprint.purpose: A year-end report from a student team captain to the school's Student Activities Board, which will vote on whether to fund the robotics club for a second year
blueprint.audience: The Harlow Creek High School Student Activities Board: a faculty-and-student committee that allocates club budgets and values participation, learning outcomes, and careful use of money
blueprint.claim: In its first season the Gearhounds built a working robot, turned beginners into capable builders, and need only modest funding to continue
blueprint.genre: report on a school project draft
blueprint.theme: the first season of a school robotics team
blueprint.speaker: Teodor Vasquez-Lindqvist, a tenth grader and captain of the Gearhounds robotics team
blueprint.exigence: The Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before its budget vote
blueprint.context: The team began in August in the woodshop with donated equipment and competed in April at the fictional Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore
blueprint.line_of_reasoning: Narrative opening establishes starting point and result; paragraph 2 traces the build process and a solved problem; paragraph 3 asserts learning and attendance; paragraph 4 lists needs and closes with a plea
blueprint.counterargument: Not addressed in the draft; the board might see a new club as an unproven expense

devices.function: Frames the season as a before-and-after story to make the result vivid
Shows the sequence of the build so the board can see steady progress
Links a failure to a diagnosed cause to show problem-solving
Contrasts a large request with a small one to make the ask seem modest

planned_flaws.flaw: Vague thesis that makes no claim and does not preview the report's organization
planned_flaws.repair_type: replace with a thesis that requires proof and previews three sections

planned_flaws.flaw: Casual, slangy wording inappropriate for a formal report to a budget committee
Claim that members learned a great deal is asserted without specific evidence
planned_flaws.repair_type: add a sentence with concrete evidence of learning

planned_flaws.flaw: Comma splice joining two independent clauses
Appeal rests on popularity and bravado rather than on values the board holds (participation, learning, frugality)
Problem-solving moment lacks a comparison that would make the team's method clear to non-engineers
planned_flaws.repair_type: add an analogy that advances the argument

provenance.venue_alias: Harlow Creek High School Student Activities Board report
provenance.note: Entirely fictional writer, school, team, competition, and figures.

set.title: The Gearhounds: A First-Season Report
paragraphs: Last August, eleven students and one chemistry teacher met in the back corner of the woodshop at Harlow Creek High School with a donated toolbox, two secondhand motor kits, and no idea how to build a robot.
Eight months later, our robot, which we named Marmalade because of its orange zip ties, placed ninth out of twenty-six teams at the Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore.
This report is about what the Gearhounds did this year and some things that happened.
I am writing it because the Student Activities Board asked every new club for a summary before it votes on next year's budgets.
The team spent September and October learning basics: how to wire a motor controller, how to read a gear ratio, how to keep a chassis from twisting.
Our first drive base, finished in November, could not turn left.
Instead of starting over, we traced the problem to a mismatched pair of wheels and swapped them in a single afternoon.
By February, Marmalade could lift a foam block, drive over a ramp, and park itself inside a taped square, the three tasks the competition required.
Honestly, the judges were kind of blown away that a first-year team even showed up with a working bot.
The members learned a great deal from the season.
Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
Our faculty adviser, Ms. Delacroix-Tam, kept a sign-in sheet, and attendance never dropped below nine members, even during exam week.
Next year the team needs a locking storage cabinet, a second set of batteries, and roughly 900 dollars for competition registration.
The board should fund us because robotics is obviously the coolest club at the school and everyone knows it.
We are not asking for a new room or a new teacher; we are asking for a shelf, a charger, and a chance to finish what we started.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 that provides specific evidence for the claim that the members learned a great deal during the season. Which sentence best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The season was long and demanding, and members gave up many Saturdays and several holiday breaks to keep working on Marmalade.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Offers evidence of effort and commitment, not of what members learned, so it supports a different claim.

options.text: Research consistently shows that hands-on clubs like robotics teach students more than classroom lectures do, which is why nearly every school funds them.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a generic, unsourced claim about clubs and schools in general and says nothing about these particular members.

options.text: Learning a great deal is the main reason any club deserves the school's financial support, which the board should remember.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Functions as commentary about why learning matters rather than as evidence that learning occurred.

options.text: Two members who could not define a gear ratio in September wrote the technical notebook that the judges scored in April.
options.label: correct
options.why: Gives a concrete before-and-after example of skill growth in named terms that directly supports the claim about learning.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that uses a comparison to help board members unfamiliar with engineering understand the team's approach, and that advances the argument that the team learned to solve problems efficiently. Which sentence best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A mismatched wheel pair is a common error in beginner builds, according to the instruction booklet that came with the kit.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Explains the error rather than comparing the approach, and shifts attention to the mistake instead of the problem-solving.

options.text: Like a team that forfeits rather than finishes, we knew from the start that quitting was always an option for us.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: The comparison contradicts sentence 7, which shows the team persisting, and undercuts the argument about efficient problem-solving.

options.text: Like a mechanic who checks the tires before rebuilding the engine, we had learned to look for the simplest explanation first.
options.label: correct
options.why: Offers a familiar analogy that clarifies the method in sentence 7 and frames it as a learned, efficient habit.

options.text: Robots, like people, have good days and bad days, and November was simply a bad month for Marmalade and its builders.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Has the form of a comparison but says nothing about how the team diagnosed or fixed the problem.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 9 so that it reports the judges' reaction in a tone appropriate for a formal report to the Student Activities Board without overstating what happened. Which version best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The adjudicating personnel expressed considerable astonishment regarding the operational status of our apparatus, a sentiment they conveyed with notable effusiveness upon its arrival.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Swings to inflated, stilted diction that sounds pompous and does not match the plain voice of the rest of the report.

options.text: Two of the judges told our adviser that they had not expected a first-year team to arrive with a fully functioning robot.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses measured, specific wording suited to a formal report and attributes the reaction to particular judges without exaggeration.

options.text: Honestly, the judges were pretty shocked that a rookie team like ours even pulled off a working bot at its first competition.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Retains the casual, conversational register of the original, including slang like 'pulled off' and 'bot.'

options.text: Every judge at the competition agreed that Marmalade was the most impressive robot of the day, and several asked to photograph it.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Replaces the casual tone with sweeping claims the writer cannot support, especially given the ninth-place finish in sentence 2.

items.stem: The writer wants to correct the punctuation of sentence 11 so that its two independent clauses are properly joined while the original meaning is preserved. Which version accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, however, by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A conjunctive adverb set off by commas cannot join two independent clauses; the comma splice remains.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before by March, they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Moves 'by March' to the first clause, changing the meaning, and still leaves a comma splice.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before; by March they were teaching the eighth graders who visited on shadow day.
options.label: correct
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses and keeps 'by March' attached to the teaching.

options.text: Several of the students who joined had never used a power drill before, by March, they were teaching the eighth graders, who visited on shadow day.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Adds commas but never supplies a semicolon or coordinating conjunction, so the two clauses are still spliced.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence at the end of the report, after sentence 15, that closes by reminding the Student Activities Board of the season's concrete results and connecting them to the modest request. Which sentence best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: A team that turned a robot that could not turn left into a ninth-place finisher on donated parts has shown what a small investment can return.
options.label: correct
options.why: Recalls specific results from the report (the November failure, ninth place, donated equipment) and ties them to the idea of a small investment, which fits the board's concern with careful spending.

options.text: Robotics is the future, and every school that ignores it will be left behind by the schools that take it seriously.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Moves to a sweeping, unsupported claim about schools in general instead of the Gearhounds' own results.

options.text: Thank you for reading this report, and please feel free to stop by the woodshop if you have any questions at all.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: A polite sign-off that mentions no results and does not link them to the funding request.

options.text: Marmalade got its name from the orange zip ties that held most of its wiring together during the whole season.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Repeats a minor detail from sentence 2 and has nothing to do with the request.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 14 so that the appeal rests on values the Student Activities Board holds: participation, learning, and careful use of money. Which version best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The board should fund us because steady attendance and new skills came from very little money, and the funding would build on both.
options.label: correct
options.why: Names all three of the board's values (participation, learning, frugality) and links them to the request.

options.text: The board should fund us because robotics is clearly more exciting than the other clubs asking for money this spring.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Keeps the competitive, boastful appeal instead of pointing to the board's values.

options.text: The board should fund us because the team had so much fun this year and would love to keep the good times going.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Hints at enthusiasm, but it says nothing about learning or careful spending.

options.text: The board should fund us because next year we plan to win the whole Tri-County Build Challenge in Dunmore outright.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Makes a promise the report gives no evidence for, and it ignores the board's values.

spec.theme: restoring a wetland near a suburb

blueprint.purpose: To convince classmates and their families to back the town council's plan to restore a drained marsh
blueprint.audience: Students, parents and teachers who read the school newspaper, Larkfield Regional High
blueprint.claim: Larkfield should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh because it would reduce flooding, control mosquitoes naturally and give students an outdoor lab.
blueprint.theme: restoring a wetland near a suburb

planned_flaws.flaw: vague thesis that states no position
planned_flaws.repair_type: replace with a specific arguable claim

planned_flaws.flaw: casual conclusion with no call to action

set.title: Let Cutler's Marsh Flood Again
paragraphs: Behind the Brambleton subdivision, past the last cul-de-sac, lies a flat field of cattails and cracked drainage pipe that most of us have never noticed.
Forty years ago it was Cutler's Marsh, until a developer dug ditches to dry it out for houses that were never built.
Wetlands are important for many reasons.
This spring the Larkfield town council will vote on whether to spend 180,000 dollars to fill those ditches and let the marsh hold water again.
Restoring the marsh would definitely end flooding in Brambleton forever.
Last April, after two days of rain, water reached the doorsteps on Finch Lane, and the town paid 64,000 dollars to pump out basements.
A marsh works like a sponge, soaking up runoff and releasing it slowly.
Some residents totally freak out about mosquitoes.
An ecologist hired by the town, Ilse Varga, reported that a healthy marsh draws dragonflies and frogs that eat mosquito larvae.
Our biology classes could use the marsh as an outdoor lab, measuring water quality instead of just reading about it.
Anyway, the council should totally go for it, because it's a no-brainer.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 11 with a conclusion that suits a school newspaper audience and urges readers to take a specific action before the vote. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Cutler's Marsh has quite a history, and it will be interesting to watch what the council finally decides.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Observes rather than urging any action.

options.text: Seriously, anyone who votes against the marsh plan is clueless and should just stay home this spring.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Insulting and slangy, unfit for a respectful editorial.

options.text: Our biology teachers already have lab equipment, so outdoor water testing would cost the school nothing.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Adds a new unsupported claim rather than concluding with a call to action.

options.text: Before the spring vote, ask your parents to write the council and support bringing Cutler's Marsh back.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses an appropriate tone and gives readers a concrete action tied to the vote.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 5 so that the claim about flooding is qualified to match the evidence in sentences 6 and 7. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Restoring the marsh would likely reduce the flooding that Brambleton suffers after heavy rains.
options.label: correct
options.why: Softens the absolute claim to one the sponge explanation and flood example can support.

options.text: Restoring the marsh would probably have no real effect on flooding along Finch Lane at all.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Contradicts the writer's argument and evidence.

options.text: Restoring the marsh would certainly stop all flooding in Brambleton and the rest of Larkfield.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Makes the claim even more absolute and widens its scope.

options.text: Restoring the marsh might perhaps help with water in a few places now and then.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Qualifies the claim but hedges so heavily that it no longer makes a useful point.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 8 so that it presents residents' concern respectfully, in a tone suited to a newspaper read by parents and teachers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Some residents are freaking out big time about a bunch of mosquitoes.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Keeps slang that dismisses the concern.

options.text: Some paranoid residents irrationally panic over the idea of mosquitoes.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Insults residents rather than presenting them respectfully.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 1 with an opening that draws school newspaper readers in by linking the forgotten field to a place they know, while keeping the focus on the marsh. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: If you have ever cut through the Brambleton cul-de-sacs on your way to school, you have walked past a field of cattails and cracked pipe that few of us have noticed.
options.label: correct
options.why: Speaks directly to student readers through a familiar route and still sets up the field that sentence 2 identifies as the marsh.

options.text: Since the beginning of human history, people have drained wetlands for farms and towns, and they have often come to regret the choices they made.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: A sweeping historical claim that loses the local, familiar hook and the specific field.

options.text: Finch Lane residents still remember the two days of rain last April, when water crept up to their doorsteps and their basements had to be pumped out.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Moves the flooding evidence in sentence 6 to the start, so the field that sentence 2 calls Cutler's Marsh is never introduced.

options.text: Honestly, most of us could not care less about some swampy old field behind a subdivision, but maybe we should start caring about it a little.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Too casual and dismissive for a paper read by parents and teachers, and it never names the place.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 6 that addresses parents who may worry about the cost of the project to taxpayers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: At that rate, the 180,000-dollar restoration would cost about as much as three floods like last April's, and the town would not have to pay it again.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses the figures from sentences 4 and 6 to answer a cost worry with a comparison taxpayers can follow.

options.text: Parents should stop worrying about money, because protecting nature is always worth whatever it ends up costing the town and its taxpayers.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Brushes off the audience's concern instead of answering it, and the claim is not supported.

options.text: The water on Finch Lane was muddy and cold, and several families had to move furniture to the upper floors of their homes that weekend.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Adds vivid detail about the flood but says nothing about cost to taxpayers.

options.text: Restoring the marsh would also save the town money on mowing, road salt and school supplies for many decades after the project is done.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Claims savings that nothing in the draft backs up, and school supplies have nothing to do with the project.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 3 with a thesis that takes a clear position and previews the three benefits discussed in the rest of the editorial. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh, because it would ease flooding, keep mosquitoes in check and give our biology classes an outdoor lab.
options.label: correct
options.why: Takes an arguable position and previews flooding, mosquitoes and the lab, in the order the paragraphs follow.

options.text: Cutler's Marsh was once home to many plants and animals, and people in Larkfield have had different opinions about its future over time.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: States no position and previews none of the editorial's points.

options.text: The town should pay to restore Cutler's Marsh, mainly because doing so would finally put an end to the flooding on Finch Lane.
options.label: too_narrow
options.why: Takes a position but previews only flooding, leaving out mosquitoes and the lab.

options.text: Although restoring Cutler's Marsh would ease flooding, the costs and the mosquitoes mean the town council should think twice about it.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Argues against the plan the editorial supports.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that explains how the sponge comparison connects to the flooding described in sentence 6. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Had the marsh been holding water last April, much of that rain would have soaked into it slowly instead of rushing toward Finch Lane.
options.label: correct
options.why: Applies the sponge comparison to the April flood, linking the evidence to the claim.

options.text: Sponges are simple sea animals, and some kinds can soak up many times their own weight in water before they release it.
options.label: lexical_trap
options.why: Picks up the word sponge but drifts to biology facts with no link to the flood.

options.text: Many other towns have restored marshes over the years, and residents there are often quite proud of the work they did.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Changes the subject to other towns instead of explaining the connection.

options.text: The ditches dug forty years ago, though, are the reason the field is so dry and cracked today, as readers may recall.
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Looks back to sentence 2's history and never ties the sponge to the April flooding.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a phrase at the beginning of sentence 10 (adjusting capitalization as needed) to show that the outdoor lab is one more benefit added to those already discussed. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Beyond controlling floods and mosquitoes,
options.label: correct
options.why: Marks the lab as an extra benefit on top of the earlier two.

options.text: Despite controlling floods and mosquitoes,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Signals contrast where the writer is adding a benefit.

options.text: As a result of the flooding,
options.label: illogical_relationship
options.why: Wrongly makes the lab a result of the flooding.

options.text: On the other hand, for students,
options.label: reversal
options.why: Sets up an opposing point instead of one more benefit.

items.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 10 with a concrete example showing how the marsh would offer hands-on learning that a textbook cannot. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Students could test the water each month and compare the samples before and after storms, seeing for themselves how a wetland filters runoff.
options.label: correct
options.why: Gives a specific hands-on activity that a textbook cannot replace.

options.text: Learning is important, and students deserve good opportunities to explore science in many different ways during their years in school.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Too general; it offers no concrete marsh activity.

options.text: Our textbooks already include detailed chapters on wetlands, with clear diagrams of water cycles and many color photos of marsh animals.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Suggests textbooks are already enough, which undercuts the point.

options.text: The marsh could also become a popular spot for families to walk dogs, watch birds and take photos on quiet weekend mornings.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Describes recreation, not learning.

items.stem: The writer wants to combine sentences 1 and 2 clearly and concisely, keeping both the field's location and the fact that it was once a marsh. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field of cattails that was, forty years ago, Cutler's Marsh, until a developer drained it for houses never built.
options.label: correct
options.why: Keeps the location, the history and the cause in one clear, concise sentence.

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision lies a field, it was Cutler's Marsh forty years ago, until a developer drained it for houses that were never built.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A comma splice joins two independent clauses.

options.text: A developer forty years ago drained a field for houses never built that lies behind the Brambleton subdivision and was Cutler's Marsh.
options.label: partially_right
options.why: Keeps the facts, but the modifiers are misplaced, so it sounds as if the houses lie behind the subdivision.

options.text: Behind the Brambleton subdivision there lies, past the very last cul-de-sac, a field that in the past, about forty years ago, was once Cutler's Marsh.
options.label: wrong_scope
options.why: Wordy and repetitive, and it leaves out the developer's draining.

items.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 7 into two independent clauses: "A marsh works like a sponge" and "it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly." Which choice joins them correctly?

options.label: correct
options.why: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses.

options.text: A marsh works like a sponge, it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly.
options.label: convention_error

options.text: A marsh works like a sponge it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: Run-on sentence with no punctuation between the clauses.

options.text: A marsh works like a sponge; and it soaks up runoff and releases it slowly.
options.label: convention_error
options.why: A semicolon followed by a conjunction is incorrect here.

items.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 11 with a conclusion that suits a school newspaper audience and urges readers to take a specific action before the vote. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?

options.text: Cutler's Marsh has quite a history, and it will be interesting to watch what the council finally decides.
options.label: wrong_function
options.why: Observes rather than urging any action.

options.text: Seriously, anyone who votes against the marsh plan is clueless and should just stay home this spring.
options.label: wrong_tone
options.why: Insulting and slangy, unfit for a respectful editorial.

options.text: Our biology teachers already have lab equipment, so outdoor water testing would cost the school nothing.
options.label: unsupported
options.why: Adds a new unsupported claim rather than concluding with a call to action.

options.text: Before the spring vote, ask your parents to write the council and support bringing Cutler's Marsh back.
options.label: correct
options.why: Uses an appropriate tone and gives readers a concrete action tied to the vote.
